lead: Close a thin wall into a loop and twist it. The torque is carried by a shear flow q that is the same all round the wall. This is the Bredt-Batho result. The wall stress depends on q and the local thickness. The twist rate depends on the area enclosed by the wall and on the integral of ds/t round the loop. Aircraft wing boxes and fuselage barrels use this idea. It turns a hard torsion problem into two or three numbers.
prereq: You need: shear flow q from 5.1, and the shaft torque-twist relation from Unit 2.

sections.h3: Constant shear flow round a closed loop

blocks.text: Take a single-cell tube. The mean line is the midline of the wall. It encloses area A (mm²). A pure torque T (N·mm) acts about the tube axis. In a thin closed wall the shear flow q (N/mm) is constant round the loop. There are no free edges, so the flow has nowhere to start or stop. It runs continuously round the wall.

Find q by taking moments about any point P inside the loop. On a length ds (mm) of wall the shear force is q ds. Its moment arm about P is r (mm). The small moment is dT = q r ds. The triangle with sides r and ds has area ½ r ds, so r ds = 2 dA. Integrate round the loop: T = q ∮ r ds = 2 A q. Hence q = T/(2A).

The wall shear stress is τ = q/t = T/(2At). t (mm) is the local wall thickness. τ (N/mm² or MPa) is largest where the wall is thinnest. A is the area enclosed by the mean line, not the outer contour. The formula assumes a thin wall, a closed loop, constant q, free warping and no buckling. Some syllabi call this Bredt's formula.

blocks.where: q is shear flow (N/mm); T is torque (N·mm); A is area enclosed by the mean line (mm²); t is wall thickness (mm); τ is wall shear stress (N/mm²).

sections.h3: Twist rate and equivalent torsion constant

blocks.text: The shear strain in the wall is γ = τ/G = q/(Gt). G (N/mm²) is the shear modulus. The twist per unit length dθ/dz (rad/mm) of a closed cell is the wall strain integrated round the loop, divided by twice the enclosed area: dθ/dz = (1/(2A))∮ γ ds. Put γ = q/(Gt) and q = T/(2A): dθ/dz = (T/(4A²G))∮(ds/t).

The integral ∮(ds/t) is taken along the mean line and is dimensionless when s and t use the same unit. For constant t and perimeter L, it is L/t. The equivalent torsion constant is J = 4A²/∮(ds/t). Then dθ/dz = T/(GJ), the same form as a solid shaft.

Check against a circular tube of mean radius R and thickness t. A = πR² and ∮ds/t = 2πR/t, so J = 2πR³t. The wall stress is τ = T/(2πR²t). The solid shaft formula τ = T r/J gives the same stress at r = R when J is taken as the polar moment of the thin ring. The symbols look alike; the meanings are different.

blocks.where: dθ/dz is twist per unit length (rad/mm); T is torque (N·mm); A is enclosed area (mm²); G is shear modulus (N/mm²); s is distance along the mean line (mm); t is wall thickness (mm); J is equivalent torsion constant (mm⁴).

sections.h3: How to use it, and when it fails

blocks.text: Use the formula in this order. Mark the mean line. Compute A from that line. Compute ∮(ds/t), splitting the loop into lengths of constant thickness. Find q = T/(2A). Find τ at each thickness. Find J and the twist rate. For a single cell the shear flow is the same in every wall.

items: Draw the mean line through the middle of each wall.
Measure A enclosed by the mean line.
Split the loop where t changes and sum each length divided by its thickness.
Use q = T/(2A) and τ = q/t.

blocks.text: The theory fails if the wall is not thin, if the loop is open, or if the wall buckles. An open section has a free edge and a different torsion law; see 5.10. A multi-cell box needs one shear flow per cell and equal twist between cells; see 5.5. Warping restraint and tapered walls need more than Bredt-Batho.

figure.caption: Torque T sets a constant shear flow q round the loop; the wall stress uses q and t, and the twist rate uses the integral of ds/t. The numbers are the worked example.

examples.question: An elliptical wing box has a mean-line area A = 0.25 m², mean perimeter L = 1.8 m, skin thickness t = 2 mm and G = 27 GPa. It carries a torque T = 40 kN·m. Find the shear flow q, the shear stress τ in the skin, the equivalent torsion constant J, and the twist per metre of span.
steps: Convert: A = 0.25 m² = 0.25 × 10⁶ mm² = 2.50 × 10⁵ mm²; L = 1.8 m = 1800 mm; T = 40 kN·m = 40 × 10⁶ N·mm; G = 27 GPa = 27 000 N/mm².
examples.answer: The shear flow is 80 N/mm, the skin shear stress is 40 MPa, the equivalent torsion constant is 277777778 mm⁴, and the twist is 0.005333 rad/m.
examples.check:
T = 40e6
A = 0.25e6
t = 2.0
L = 1800.0
G = 27000.0
q = T/(2*A)
tau = q/t
integral = L/t
J = 4*A*A/integral
twist_per_m = T/(G*J)*1000
print(f'{q:.1f}')
print(f'{tau:.1f}')
print(f'{J:.0f}')
print(f'{twist_per_m:.6f}')

traps: Using the outer contour area instead of the area enclosed by the mean line makes A too large and q and τ too small.
Applying Bredt-Batho to an open section: an open wall twists by the St Venant law, not by q = T/(2A); see 5.10.
Forgetting that q is constant only for a single closed cell under pure torque. A multi-cell section has a different q in each cell; see 5.5.
Taking ∮(ds/t) as perimeter/t when t changes: split the loop and add each length divided by its own thickness.
Mixing units: T in N·m with A in mm² gives q wrong by 1000; convert torque to N·mm first.

quiz.q: State the Bredt-Batho formula for shear flow in a closed thin-walled tube. Define each symbol.
quiz.a: q = T/(2A), where q is shear flow (N/mm), T is torque (N·mm), and A is the area enclosed by the mean line (mm²).

quiz.q: Why is q constant round a single closed loop under pure torque?
quiz.a: There is no free edge, so the shear flow cannot start or stop. Moment equilibrium about a point inside the loop then gives T = 2Aq, so q = T/(2A) is the same in every wall.

quiz.q: A closed tube has A = 50000 mm², t = 1.5 mm and T = 12 kN·m. Find q and τ.
The same tube has L = 1000 mm and G = 27000 N/mm². Find J and the twist per metre.
A wing box has thin skin and thicker spar walls. Under pure torque, where is τ largest and why?
quiz.a: τ = q/t and q is the same all round a single cell. Therefore τ is largest where t is smallest, which is the thin skin.

quiz.q: A student uses the outer contour area in place of the mean-line area. What happens to q, τ and twist?
quiz.a: A_outer > A_mean. q = T/(2A) is lower, so τ = q/t is lower. J = 4A²/∮ds/t is larger, so the twist is lower. The section looks stronger than it is.

quiz.q: Show that a circular tube of mean radius R and thickness t has J = 2πR³t.

beyond: Not for the exam. Aircraft wing torsion boxes are usually multi-cell, so the single-cell result is the building block rather than the final tool. Finite-element codes solve the same problem with shell elements and can include warping restraint, tapering and buckling. Composite wing skins add anisotropy: the shear stiffness G is direction-dependent, so the integral ∮(ds/t) becomes an integral of a stiffness-weighted wall. Search next for Bredt-Batho torsion, equivalent torsion constant, multi-cell torsion, and warping restraint in closed-section beams.
